cues.x: Good to Great, by Jim Collins.
Good is the enemy of great.
That is the very first line of this book, and Jim Collins means it as a diagnosis of why so little in the world becomes truly excellent.
We do not have great schools, he says, principally because we have good schools.
We do not have great government, principally because we have good government.
Very few people attain a great life, in large part because it is so easy to settle for a good one.
Good is comfortable.
Good is enough to keep going.
And precisely because good is available and acceptable, it becomes the thing that stops us from ever reaching for great.
So Collins set out to answer a question that had been nagging at him.
Can a merely good company become a genuinely great one, and if so, how?

Is greatness reserved for a lucky few blessed from birth with the right genetics and the right circumstances, or is it something that can be built, deliberately, by understanding what actually causes it?
The book actually began with an insult, which is my favorite kind of origin story.
Collins had already written a bestseller called Built to Last, about enduring great companies.

He was having dinner with a McKinsey consultant named Bill Meehan, and Meehan said, in the pleasant way consultants deliver bad news, that he and his colleagues loved Built to Last but found it useless.
Because, he said, the companies you studied were great practically from the beginning.
They had founders like David Packard and George Merck who shaped the character of greatness from the earliest days.
Most of us run companies that are pretty good but not great.
And we have no idea how to change that.
Collins sat with the question for a long time and eventually admitted Meehan was right.
Built to Last was the sequel.
The prequel had never been written.
How does a good company, an average company, even a bad one, achieve enduring greatness?
So he assembled a team and spent five years finding out.
To answer that, he did something that took five years and a team of researchers, and I want you to appreciate how rigorous it was, because the rigor is what makes the conclusions trustworthy.
He and his team combed through the entire history of the Fortune 500, looking for a very specific and demanding pattern.

They wanted companies that had shown fifteen years of merely good, ordinary results, right in line with the general market, and then, at some transition point, broke through and produced fifteen years of truly extraordinary results, at least three times the general stock market.
Not a lucky spike, but a sustained, fifteen-year transformation.
And then, crucially, they insisted the transformation be independent of the industry.
It could not just be that the whole industry got hot.
The company had to leap while its direct competitors did not.
Out of the entire universe of major American companies, only eleven met this brutal standard.
Eleven companies that went from good to great and stayed there.
Names like Walgreens, the drugstore chain.
Kimberly-Clark, the paper company.
Nucor, the steelmaker.
Wells Fargo.
Gillette.
Kroger.
Abbott Laboratories.
Circuit City, which was great during the study period.
Companies that were, on the surface, unglamorous, ordinary, the kind you would never put in a book about greatness.
But their results were staggering.
If you had invested one dollar in the good-to-great companies at their transition point, that dollar would have massively outperformed the market, often by a factor of many times over.
And here is the part that makes the study so powerful.

For every one of those eleven great companies, Collins found a comparison company, a direct competitor in the same industry, with the same opportunities and the same resources at the same moment in history, that did not make the leap.
So now he had a controlled experiment.
Same industry, same era, same conditions.
One company became great, the other stayed merely good.
Whatever was different between them could not be explained by luck, or industry, or timing.
It had to be something the great companies did.
Collins told his team to go in with no theory, to let the data speak, to resist their own assumptions.
And what came back surprised even him.
Many of the things we assume drive greatness turned out to be irrelevant, or even the opposite of what works.
Let me walk you through what the great companies actually had in common, because the pattern is consistent, and it is not what you would expect.
It starts at the top, with leadership, and this was the first surprise, one Collins says his team actually resisted at first.
He had told them explicitly to downplay the role of top executives, because he was tired of the simplistic story that credits or blames the CEO for everything.

But the data kept shoving leadership back in his face, and when they looked closely at what kind of leader ran these companies through their transitions, they found something that shattered the usual image.
The leaders who took companies from good to great were not the larger-than-life, celebrity, charismatic saviors that magazines put on their covers.
They were, almost without exception, quiet, humble, self-effacing, even shy.
Collins calls them Level 5 leaders, the top of a hierarchy of leadership capability, and the defining trait of a Level 5 leader is a paradoxical blend of two things that rarely go together.
Extreme personal humility, and intense professional will.
They are ferociously ambitious, but here is the key, the ambition is for the company and its cause, not for themselves.
The story he tells to make this real is about Darwin Smith, the CEO who led Kimberly-Clark through its transformation.
Smith was a mild-mannered man, an in-house lawyer, who once described himself as never stopping trying to become qualified for the job.
He was awkward, wore unfashionable suits, shunned the spotlight, spent his vacations doing farm work.
And yet this unassuming man made one of the most ferociously bold decisions in the history of American business.
Kimberly-Clark's core business for a hundred years had been coated paper, running paper mills.

But Smith concluded, after confronting the hard truth, that the paper business was mediocre and always would be, and that the company's real future lay in consumer products, in competing directly with the toughest company in the world, Procter and Gamble.
So he did something almost unthinkable.
He sold the mills.
He sold the company's historic core, the very identity of the business, and threw all the proceeds into building consumer brands like Kleenex and Huggies.
The business press called it stupid.
Wall Street was skeptical.

But Smith had the will to do what was right for the company's long-term greatness regardless of how it looked, and Kimberly-Clark went on to beat Procter and Gamble and become the number one paper-based consumer products company in the world.
That is the Level 5 combination.
The humility to subordinate his ego, and the iron will to make the brutal, correct decision.
There is a detail about Darwin Smith that Collins puts almost in passing, and it stops you cold.
Two months after Smith became CEO, doctors diagnosed him with nose and throat cancer and told him he had less than a year to live.

He informed the board, made clear he had no intention of dying and no intention of resigning, and then kept working a full schedule while driving weekly from Wisconsin to Houston for radiation treatment.
He lived twenty five more years, twenty of them as chief executive.
That is the will half of the equation.
And when a reporter later pressed him on the secret of his extraordinary run, all this mild man would say was that he had never stopped trying to become qualified for the job.
That is the humility half.
The word Level 5 comes from a hierarchy Collins sketches, and it helps to see the whole ladder.
Level 1 is a highly capable individual, someone who makes productive contributions through talent, knowledge and good work habits.
Level 2 is a contributing team member, who works effectively with others toward group objectives.
Level 3 is a competent manager, who organizes people and resources toward objectives.
Level 4 is an effective leader, who catalyzes commitment to a clear and compelling vision and drives high performance standards.
Most admired executives, and plenty of famous ones, top out here.
Level 5 sits above all of it, and it does not replace the lower levels, it sits on top of them.
What makes it different is not more charisma or more brilliance.
It is that the ambition points outward, at the institution, rather than inward, at the self.
The second great Level 5 story in the book is Colman Mockler of Gillette.
In the middle of the nineteen eighties, Gillette faced three hostile takeover attempts, two from Ronald Perelman of Revlon.
Any shareholder could have cashed out at a large immediate premium by taking the deal.
Mockler was a reserved, gracious man who had never sought the spotlight, and he could easily have taken the money and retired rich and comfortable.

Instead he fought, because he believed the company was about to reap enormous returns from massive investments it had already made in shaving systems that were not yet on the market, the Sensor and later the Mach3.
He personally called hundreds of individual investors, many of them elderly, to explain the case.
He won.

And Collins notes that shareholders who took the buyout money and invested it in the general market for the next decade ended up with less than a third of what they would have had by sticking with Mockler's Gillette.
Then comes the detail that makes the story unforgettable.
In January nineteen ninety one, Gillette launched the Sensor, and Mockler was on his way to review the proof of a Forbes cover story about the company's triumph.
Walking down the hall, he suffered a massive heart attack and died, almost instantly, still holding the pages.
The cover carried a big word: triumph.
Collins uses it as a portrait of a man whose ambition was entirely for the institution he served, right up to the last minute of his life.
The contrast cases are just as instructive.
Collins points to leaders who built spectacular personal reputations while leaving their companies worse off.

Lee Iacocca dramatically rescued Chrysler in the first half of his tenure, and then, in the second half, spent his energy on his own celebrity, the talk shows, the autobiography that sold millions, even a flirtation with running for president, while Chrysler's performance slid back toward the bottom.
Al Dunlap of Scott Paper cut ferociously, sold the company off, and then wrote a book celebrating himself as a corporate Rambo.
Collins also found a telling pattern in succession.
Level 5 leaders set up their successors for even greater success, because their ambition was for the company to keep winning after they were gone.
A striking number of the comparison leaders set their successors up to fail, sometimes appointing weak heirs, which is, if you think about it, the ultimate act of ego.
What better way to prove your own greatness than for the place to fall apart the moment you leave.
Collins gives you a wonderful way to spot the difference between a Level 5 leader and a merely egotistical one.
He calls it the window and the mirror.
When things go well, the Level 5 leader looks out the window, pointing to other people, to good luck, to factors outside themselves, giving away the credit.
But when things go badly, they look in the mirror, taking full responsibility, never blaming bad luck or other people.
The comparison leaders, the ego-driven ones, did exactly the reverse.
When things went well, they looked in the mirror, taking the credit for themselves.
When things went badly, they looked out the window, blaming everyone and everything else.
That simple test, where do you point in success and where do you point in failure, reveals the whole character of a leader.
Now, having found the right kind of leader, you might expect that the next step in a transformation would be to set a bold new vision and strategy, to decide where the company is going.
But Collins found the great companies did the opposite, and this is the second big idea, one he captures in a phrase that has become famous.
First who, then what.
Before they figured out where to drive the bus, the good-to-great leaders first got the right people on the bus, and the wrong people off the bus, and the right people in the right seats.
Then, and only then, did they figure out where to drive it.
The conventional wisdom says you start with a vision and a strategy and then find people to execute it.
The great companies flipped that.
They believed that if you begin with who rather than what, you can adapt far better to a changing world.
If people join the bus mainly because of where it is going, what happens when you have to change direction?
But if people are on the bus because of who else is on it, then the destination can change and they will still be committed.
There is a deeper logic here that Collins draws out.
When you have the right people, the great, self-motivated, self-disciplined people, then many of your management problems simply evaporate.
You do not need to spend enormous energy motivating them or tightly controlling them, because the right people are internally driven to produce the best results.
And when you have the wrong people, no amount of vision or incentive fixes it.
He is also blunt about being rigorous, not ruthless.
Rigorous means you hold high standards at all levels, and when you know you have the wrong person, you act.
But he says the great companies were actually more humane, because letting the wrong person linger in a job they cannot do well is unfair to them and to everyone forced to compensate for them.
And he offers a piece of practical wisdom for when you are unsure whether to let someone go.
Ask yourself, if it were a hiring decision rather than a firing decision, would you hire this person again?
If the answer is no, and the only reason you are keeping them is that letting them go would be uncomfortable, you already know what to do.
He also notes that the great companies put their best people on their biggest opportunities, not their biggest problems.
The story he uses is Wells Fargo, and it is a beautiful illustration of getting the who right before you can possibly know the what.

In the early nineteen seventies, the chief executive Dick Cooley could see that banking deregulation was coming, but nobody, including him, had the faintest idea what the industry would look like on the other side.
His response was not to write a strategy for a world he could not predict.

His response was to hire relentlessly, injecting the best people he could find anywhere, often without any specific job in mind for them, on the theory that when the storm arrived he would need the best crew in banking on his boat.
He was right.
When deregulation hit and chaos followed, Wells Fargo had, by common consent, the strongest management bench in the industry, and Carl Reichardt drove it through the transition.
The comparison company, Bank of America, took the opposite approach.

It was described as following a weak generals, strong lieutenants model, promoting people who would not rock the boat, and when deregulation broke over the industry it lurched, lost over a billion dollars in three years, and eventually had to import a batch of Wells Fargo people to help fix it.
Collins is also careful to kill an assumption.
His team went looking, hard, for a link between executive compensation schemes and the leap from good to great, and they found nothing.
No pattern.
The great companies did not pay more, did not use more stock options, did not have cleverer bonus structures than their comparisons.
As he puts it, the purpose of compensation is not to get the right behaviors from the wrong people, it is to get the right people on the bus in the first place and keep them there.
And he distills the who question into three practical disciplines.
First, when in doubt, do not hire, keep looking.
Second, when you know you need to make a people change, act, and do not spend a year agonizing while everyone else pays the price.

Third, put your best people on your biggest opportunities, not your biggest problems, because managing your problems only makes you good, while building your opportunities is the only way to become great.
The third idea Collins calls confronting the brutal facts, and it comes wrapped in one of the most moving stories in the entire book, the story of Admiral Jim Stockdale.

Stockdale was the highest-ranking United States military officer held prisoner in Vietnam, tortured over twenty times across eight years in the prison camp known as the Hanoi Hilton, with no certainty he would survive, no idea if he would ever see his family again.
Collins had lunch with Stockdale years later and asked him how on earth he made it through.
Stockdale said, I never lost faith in the end of the story.
I never doubted that I would get out, and moreover that I would prevail in the end and turn the experience into the defining event of my life.
And then Collins asked the harder question.
Who didn't make it out?
And Stockdale answered instantly.
Oh, that's easy.
The optimists.
Collins was confused.
The optimists?
Stockdale explained.
The optimists were the ones who said, we're going to be out by Christmas.
And Christmas would come and go.
And then they would say, we're going to be out by Easter.
And Easter would come and go.
And then Thanksgiving.
And then it would be Christmas again.
And Stockdale said, they died of a broken heart.
Then Stockdale gave Collins the lesson that Collins named the Stockdale Paradox, and it is one of the most important ideas in the book.

You must never confuse faith that you will prevail in the end, which you can never afford to lose, with the discipline to confront the most brutal facts of your current reality, whatever they might be.
Hold both at once.
Unwavering faith that you will win, combined with unflinching honesty about how bad things actually are right now.
The optimists died because they had the faith but not the brutal facts.
They kept setting hopeful deadlines that reality demolished, and each demolition broke them a little more.
The survivors held onto the certainty of eventual victory while being ruthlessly realistic about the awful present.
And Collins found this exact paradox in the great companies.
They faced their brutal facts, their failing businesses, their real competitive weaknesses, without flinching and without pretending, while never losing faith that they would find a way to prevail.
He argues that leadership is not about starting with a vision and then bullying reality into fitting it.
It is about creating a climate where the truth can be heard, where facts are not shot down, where people can raise problems without being punished.
He talks about leading with questions rather than answers, engaging in real dialogue and debate rather than coercion, and conducting honest autopsies without blame.
The point of confronting brutal facts is not to become demoralized.
It is that when you rigorously face reality, the right decisions often become self-evident.
The business version of the Stockdale Paradox in this book is the tale of two grocery chains, and it is worth telling properly.
In nineteen fifty three, A and P was the largest retailing organization in the world and one of the largest companies in America, a giant.
Kroger was a modest, unremarkable chain.

Both faced exactly the same brutal fact in the following decades: the old-fashioned little grocery store was dying, and American shoppers wanted bigger stores with more variety, fresh bakeries, flowers, banking, prepared food, everything under one roof.
Kroger looked at that fact and did the hard thing.
Beginning in the early nineteen seventies it methodically set about replacing, remodeling or eliminating every single store, and it changed every region, systematically, to fit the new reality.
By nineteen ninety nine Kroger was the number one grocery chain in America.
A and P had the same information.
It even ran an experiment.
It opened a new store called the Golden Key, a different format, no A and P branding, where managers were free to try the superstore idea, and it worked.
Customers liked it.
It was telling them exactly what they needed to know.
And A and P closed it, because the answers it produced did not fit what the company wanted to believe about itself.
Instead they lurched through a decade of hopeful programs, a price-slashing campaign, cost cutting, hiring a savior chief executive, then another, then another, each with a new grand plan.
Collins says they kept looking for the one program, the one acquisition, the one fad that would work, rather than facing the truth.
A and P slid into irrelevance.
The facts were sitting in front of both companies.
One had the discipline to look.
So how do you build a place where the truth actually gets heard?
Collins gives four practices.
Lead with questions, not answers, which means walking in genuinely not knowing, and using your position to ask rather than to declare.
Engage in dialogue and debate, not coercion, real arguments, sometimes heated ones, in search of the best answer rather than a performance where everyone knows the boss has already decided.
Conduct autopsies without blame, so that a failure produces understanding rather than a scapegoat, because the moment people learn that mistakes get people punished they stop reporting them.
And build red flag mechanisms, structures that turn information into information that cannot be ignored.
His example here is a company called Graniterock and its chief executive Bruce Woolpert, who instituted a policy called short pay.

On every invoice, in print, the customer was told that if they were not satisfied they could simply deduct any amount from the bill they felt was fair, or not pay it at all, and they did not need to call or return anything.
That is not a customer satisfaction survey that can be filed away.
That is a brutal fact arriving in the accounting department every month with a number attached, impossible to spin.
Now we arrive at what is probably the most famous concept in the entire book, the Hedgehog Concept.
Collins borrows it from an old essay that divides the world into foxes and hedgehogs, based on an ancient Greek line.
The fox knows many things, but the hedgehog knows one big thing.
The fox is cunning and complex, pursuing many ends at the same time, scattering its energy, seeing the world in all its messy complexity.
The hedgehog simplifies the whole world into a single organizing idea, one basic principle that unifies and guides everything.
And when the clever fox attacks, with all its speed and cunning, the hedgehog just rolls into a ball, a perfect sphere of sharp spikes, and the fox retreats defeated.
Every single time.
Collins found that the good-to-great leaders were, to one degree or another, hedgehogs.
They took a complex world and simplified it into a single, crystalline, organizing concept.
The comparison companies were foxes, scattered, inconsistent, chasing many things at once, never boiling it down.
But the Hedgehog Concept is not just about being simple.
It is a very specific kind of understanding, and Collins pictures it as three circles that overlap.
The first circle is, what can you be the best in the world at?
Not what you want to be best at, not what you have set a goal to be best at, but what you actually can be best at, and equally important, what you cannot be best at.
The second circle is, what drives your economic engine?
Every great company found a single financial denominator, what Collins calls profit per x, that had the greatest impact on their economics, and they gained deep insight into it.
The third circle is, what are you deeply passionate about?
What lights a fire in you and your people?
And your Hedgehog Concept lives right in the center where all three circles overlap.
It is the single, simple idea that flows from the intersection of what you can be best at, what powers your economics, and what you are passionate about.
The example he uses is Walgreens, and it is beautifully humble.
Walgreens did not have some grand technological breakthrough.
Their hedgehog was this.
They could be the best in the world at convenient drugstores.
So they built the most convenient stores imaginable, clustering them so tightly that customers were never far from one, putting them on the best corners, making it effortless to run in.
And their economic engine was not profit per store, which was the obvious metric.
They discovered that the real driver was profit per customer visit.
Once they saw that, everything clicked.
Convenient locations drive more visits, more visits drive up profit per visit, and the whole model reinforces itself.
It sounds almost embarrassingly simple.
But Collins stresses that these companies took years, on average about four years, to arrive at their Hedgehog Concept.
It looks simple only after enormous effort and honest debate.
The simplicity is on the far side of complexity, not the near side.
A hedgehog concept is not a goal or a strategy or an intention to be the best.
It is an understanding of what you actually can be the best at.
The economic engine circle deserves a moment, because it is the most actionable and the most neglected.
Collins found that each great company got a piercing insight into a single denominator, a ratio in the form of profit per something, that had the greatest effect on its economics.

Walgreens switched from profit per store to profit per customer visit, and it changed everything they did, because now an expensive corner location that cannibalized an older store nearby was obviously worth it.
Wells Fargo shifted to profit per employee once it realized deregulation meant it had to run like a business rather than a bank.
Nucor drove profit per ton of finished steel.
Kimberly-Clark moved to profit per consumer brand.
Fannie Mae landed on profit per mortgage risk level, which sounds dry until you realize it meant their entire competitive edge came from understanding risk better than anyone else.
The exercise Collins wants you to do is exactly this.
If you could pick one and only one ratio, profit per x, to systematically increase over time, what x would have the greatest and most sustainable impact on your economics?
Sit with it for a while.
It is a harder question than it looks.
The best example of the first circle, of what you cannot be best at, is Abbott Laboratories.
In nineteen sixty four Abbott looked at itself honestly and admitted something painful.
It had fallen behind, and it would never, ever be the best pharmaceutical company in the world.
Merck owned that ground.
A lesser company would have set a goal to catch up anyway, because that is what everyone does.
Abbott instead asked what it could be the best at, and found an answer nobody was fighting over: creating products that make health care more cost-effective.
Hospital nutritionals, diagnostics, devices.
It was unglamorous.
It was also true.

And Collins notes that these concepts took an average of four years to emerge, usually through a mechanism the companies stumbled into, a standing group of the right people who met regularly to argue, to ask questions, to test ideas against evidence, with no pretense that anyone had the answer yet.
He calls it a Council.
Not a committee that approves things.
A group that hunts for the truth.
The fifth idea is a culture of discipline, and here Collins connects several threads.
He says that most companies, as they grow, build up bureaucracy and hierarchy to compensate for incompetence and a lack of discipline.
They add rules and controls to manage the small percentage of people who are wrong for the bus.
But that bureaucracy then drives away the right people, the disciplined, self-motivated ones who chafe under all the controls.
The great companies broke this cycle.
Because they had already gotten the right, self-disciplined people on the bus in the first place, they did not need the suffocating bureaucracy.
Instead they built a culture of discipline with three layers.
Disciplined people, who do not need to be managed.
Disciplined thought, the willingness to confront brutal facts while holding to the Hedgehog Concept.
And disciplined action, staying rigorously within the three circles.
He describes it as freedom and responsibility within a framework.
The framework is the Hedgehog Concept, and within it, disciplined people have enormous freedom to do whatever it takes.
Collins tells a small, unforgettable story to capture the flavor of this discipline, about a triathlete named Dave Scott, a six-time winner of the Ironman.
Scott trained by biking seventy-five miles, swimming twenty thousand meters, and running seventeen miles, on an average day.
And he had a belief that low-fat food gave him a competitive edge.
So Dave Scott would rinse his cottage cheese to get the extra fat off.
Rinse his cottage cheese.
There is no evidence he even needed to, but that image, of a world-class athlete rinsing every bit of fat off his cottage cheese, captures the fanatical, disciplined consistency of these companies.
They did the unglamorous, disciplined things, again and again, with a rigor that ordinary organizations simply do not sustain.
And a huge part of discipline, Collins says, is the discipline to say no.
The great companies had the discipline to not do the things that fell outside their three circles, no matter how attractive the opportunity looked.
They built what he calls stop-doing lists as seriously as most people build to-do lists.
The sixth idea is about technology, and it is another myth-buster.
In the era Collins was writing, everyone believed technology was the driving force of transformation.
But when he studied the great companies, he found that technology, by itself, was almost never the cause of either greatness or decline.
The great companies did use technology, sometimes brilliantly, and they were often pioneers in applying specific technologies.
But, and this is the key, they used technology as an accelerator of momentum, not a creator of it.
They asked a disciplined question about any new technology.
Does it fit directly with our Hedgehog Concept?
If it did, they became pioneers in applying it.
If it did not, they ignored it or adopted it at a measured pace.
Technology, Collins says, is an accelerator, not a creator.
You cannot use technology to turn a directionless company into a great one.
If you are already rolling in the right direction, the right technology pours fuel on the fire.
But it is the underlying transformation, the people and the hedgehog concept and the discipline, that creates the momentum in the first place.
The company Collins uses to show a culture of discipline at full strength is Nucor, the steelmaker, and its culture is genuinely strange in the best way.
Nucor deliberately built its mills in rural farming communities in the American South, not because land was cheap, but because it wanted farmers.
People who, as Collins puts it, get up at dawn and go do what needs doing without anyone telling them.

It then built a pay system that would terrify most organizations: work teams paid on production, with bonuses that could double or triple a base wage, and no bonus at all when the team failed to produce good steel.
If a bad batch got caught before shipping, the team lost the bonus for it.
If it got out to a customer, they lost three times that.
Steelworkers at Nucor ended up among the best paid in the industry while the company held the lowest cost per ton in the industry.
And the culture was fiercely egalitarian.

No executive dining room, no company cars, no reserved parking, no corporate jet fleet, everyone including the chief executive on the same insurance and the same vacation policy, senior executives paid a lower base salary relative to comparable firms with the upside coming from the same performance system as everyone else.
Every single employee's name was printed on the cover of the annual report.
The wrong people quit fast.
The right people stayed for decades.
The single hardest form of discipline, Collins argues, is budgeting, and he redefines it in a way that stings.
In a great company, budgeting is not about deciding how much each activity gets.
It is about deciding which activities best support the Hedgehog Concept and should be fully funded, and which should not be funded at all.
Full stop.
Not trimmed.
Not funded.
That is what Darwin Smith did when he sold the paper mills, which remains the most extreme stop-doing decision in the book: he did not trim the core business, he eliminated it.
And Collins's larger point is that most of us do not have a to-do problem.
We have a stop-doing problem.
Most of us lead busy but undisciplined lives, adding item after item, never subtracting.
The great companies used their hedgehog as the knife.
The technology story that makes this stick is Walgreens and the internet.

When the dot-com frenzy arrived, an online pharmacy called drugstore dot com launched to enormous fanfare, and the narrative was that a hundred year old chain of physical drugstores was about to be obliterated.
Walgreens stock fell by roughly forty percent.
And Walgreens, characteristically, did not panic and did not proclaim an internet strategy.
Its executives described their approach as crawl, walk, run.

They studied the technology patiently, asked how it could serve their hedgehog of convenience, and then built an online capability that connected directly to their physical stores, so you could order online and pick up at the drive-through window of a store you already passed on your way home.
That is convenience, accelerated by technology, rather than technology in search of a purpose.
Within a couple of years drugstore dot com's stock had collapsed while Walgreens quietly climbed.
The lesson is not that the internet did not matter.
It is that technology amplifies whatever you already are.
Pour it on a directionless company and you get faster directionlessness.
Which brings us to the idea that ties the whole book together, the flywheel.
Collins says that from the outside, these transformations often looked like sudden, dramatic, revolutionary breakthroughs.
One day the company was ordinary, and then, seemingly overnight, it was great.
But from the inside, it never felt that way.
There was no single defining action, no grand program, no miracle moment, no one killer innovation.
Instead, he asks you to picture a giant, heavy flywheel, a massive metal disk mounted on an axle, perhaps thirty feet across, weighing many tons.
Your job is to get it spinning as fast as possible.
You push.
At first nothing seems to happen.
You keep pushing, and after enormous effort, you get it to move one single inch.
You keep pushing, and it completes one slow rotation.
You keep pushing, and it goes a little faster.
Two turns.
Then four.
Then eight.
It keeps building.
Sixteen.
Thirty-two.
The momentum starts to work for you.
A hundred turns.
A thousand.
And then, at some point, breakthrough.
The flywheel's own weight and momentum are now on your side, and it flies forward almost unstoppably, hurling itself around turn after turn.
Now here is Collins's question.
Which one of those pushes was the one that made the flywheel go so fast?
Was it the first push?
The fiftieth?
The five-thousandth?
Of course it is an absurd question.
No single push did it.
It was all of them together, the relentless accumulation of consistent effort, all pointed in the same direction, compounding over time.
That is how good becomes great.
Not through one revolutionary act, but through a quiet, disciplined, relentless pushing of the flywheel, turn after turn after turn, until the momentum builds to breakthrough.
The greatness comes from the cumulative process, the buildup leading to breakthrough.
And the comparison companies, the ones that failed, did the opposite, in a pattern Collins calls the doom loop.

Instead of patiently building momentum, they lurched back and forth, launching dramatic new programs, changing direction, chasing the latest fad, reorganizing, bringing in a savior CEO with a bold new vision, and then, when it did not produce instant results, abandoning it and lurching to the next thing.
Push the flywheel one way, then stop, then push it the other way.
Never letting the momentum build.
Grasping for the single miracle that never comes.
And so they stayed forever ordinary, exhausting themselves in fits and starts while the great companies quietly built unstoppable momentum.
One of the strangest findings in the whole study belongs here.
When Collins's researchers interviewed the executives who had presided over these transformations, they kept asking, what was the moment?
What was the turning point, the name of the initiative, the big launch?
And the executives could not answer.
Many were genuinely puzzled by the question.
There was no launch event.
No tagline.
No transformation program with a logo.
No moment of triumph.
Several of them said some version of, well, it was obvious in hindsight, we just kept doing what made sense.
They were sitting inside a process so gradual that it did not feel like a transformation from the inside at all, right up until the results made it undeniable from the outside.
Collins also notes a favorite trap of the doom loop companies: acquisitions used as a substitute for momentum.
The great companies did make acquisitions, but almost always after their flywheel was already spinning and always inside the three circles, using deals to accelerate what was working.
The mediocre ones bought big and bought often, hoping a purchase would supply the momentum they lacked.
As Collins puts it, two great mediocrities never make one great company.
So let me gather all of this into the single arc it forms, because Collins built it as a coherent chain, and each link makes the next possible.
It begins with disciplined people.
First you get Level 5 leadership at the helm, that rare blend of deep personal humility and fierce professional will, leaders who point out the window in success and into the mirror in failure.
Then, before deciding anything about strategy, those leaders get the right people on the bus and the wrong people off, trusting that with the right who, the what will take care of itself.
Then comes disciplined thought.

Those right people confront the brutal facts of reality without ever losing faith that they will prevail, the Stockdale Paradox, and out of that honest confrontation, over years of debate, they distill their Hedgehog Concept, the single simple idea sitting where their three circles overlap, what they can be best at, what drives their economics, and what they are deeply passionate about.
Then comes disciplined action.

They build a culture of discipline, freedom within the framework of the hedgehog, doing the unglamorous right things over and over, and they use technology only as an accelerator of that hedgehog, never as a substitute for it.
And all of this together turns the flywheel, push after consistent push, buildup leading to breakthrough, until good has quietly, relentlessly, become great.
There is one last thought Collins leaves you with, and it lifts the whole book beyond business.
He says that building greatness is, in the end, no harder than settling for mediocrity.
The people who built these great companies were not working harder or suffering more than the people at the comparison companies.
In many ways they had more clarity and more peace, because they knew who they were, what they could be best at, and where they were pushing.
The tragedy is not that greatness is impossibly difficult.
The tragedy is that so many capable people, and organizations, and lives, settle for good, when great was within reach the whole time.
And greatness, he insists, is not a matter of circumstance.

It is a matter of conscious choice and discipline, of doing the unglamorous fundamentals with fanatical consistency, of getting the right people around you and facing the truth and finding your one big thing and then pushing your flywheel, day after day, with unwavering faith and unflinching honesty, until it flies.
He closes with a question people kept asking him, which is essentially, why bother?
If you already have a good company, a good career, a good life, why go through all this?
And his answer has two halves.
The first is that it is not actually more work.
Once the flywheel is turning, the great organization is a far easier and more coherent place to be than the mediocre one lurching from program to program.
The second half is the one that matters more.
If you are doing something you care about, and you believe in its purpose, then it is nearly impossible to imagine not trying to make it great.
It is simply the question of what to do with the hours you have.

Collins reminds you that this is the prequel to his earlier work: get from good to great, then apply the enduring core values and the big audacious goals of Built to Last, and you have something that outlives you.
The point is not the stock chart.

The point is that most people spend their working lives on something merely good, and the difference between good and great is not talent or luck but a set of unglamorous disciplines available to anyone who chooses them.
So let me leave you with the practical heart of it.
Look honestly at whether you point out the window when things go well and into the mirror when they go badly, and start practicing that reversal deliberately.
Before you chase any new goal, get the who right, surround yourself with the right people and let go of the wrong ones, even when it is uncomfortable.
Confront your own brutal facts, the ones you have been avoiding, while holding firm to the faith that you will prevail.

Work patiently, over weeks and months if you need to, to find your own three circles, what you can be best at, what powers your engine, and what you truly love, and let their intersection become the simple idea that guides everything.
Build a stop-doing list as seriously as your to-do list.

And above all, stop waiting for the one miracle push, and instead commit to turning your flywheel with disciplined, consistent effort, trusting that the accumulation of small, right actions is exactly how good, quietly and inevitably, becomes great.
